drug_class: Antiemetic / Substance P antagonist (NK1 receptor antagonist)
purpose: Fosaprepitant is used to help prevent nausea and vomiting caused by chemotherapy (cancer treatment). It is usually given along with other anti-nausea medicines to give you the best protection. It works before and after your chemotherapy treatment to keep you feeling as comfortable as possible.
how_it_works: When you receive chemotherapy, your body releases a natural chemical called Substance P that can trigger nausea and vomiting. Fosaprepitant blocks the receptors in your brain that respond to Substance P, which helps stop those signals from making you feel sick. It is given as an IV infusion (through a vein) and quickly converts in your body into the active medicine called aprepitant.
common_side_effects: Tiredness or weakness, hiccups, loss of appetite, constipation or diarrhea, headache, and mild irritation or pain at the IV injection site are the most common side effects. Some people may also notice dizziness or a mild rash.
warnings: Tell your doctor or pharmacist about ALL medications you take, because fosaprepitant can interact with many common drugs including blood thinners, certain antifungals, and some hormonal birth control pills — it may make birth control less effective, so use a backup method. Avoid it if you are allergic to aprepitant or fosaprepitant. It should not be used with a medicine called pimozide. Let your healthcare team know right away if you notice a severe skin reaction or signs of allergic reaction such as swelling, rash, or trouble breathing.
typical_dosing: Fosaprepitant is given by a nurse as a single IV infusion over about 30 minutes, usually on the first day of your chemotherapy cycle. The typical adult dose is 150 mg given about 30 minutes before chemotherapy starts. Your doctor will decide the exact dose and schedule that is right for you.
